summary: Source-based expansion of the category-to-space tools used by Quillen K-theory: nerves and classifying spaces, coverings and homology with local coefficients (Quillen 1973 §1; Weibel K-book IV §3), homotopy fibres, the bisimplicial realization lemma, Quillen's quasi-fibration lemma and complete proofs of Theorems A and B; acyclic maps and the plus construction (Weibel IV §1, with Hatcher's cell-attachment proof of existence); the S⁻¹S group completion, Quillen's localization-of-homology theorem, the telescope identification with Z × BGL(R)⁺ and cofinality for projective modules (Weibel IV §4); Segal's Γ-space delooping and the Eilenberg–Mac Lane bar construction (Carlsson, Handbook I.1 §1.2); the iterated S.-construction spectrum (Weibel IV §8); and mod-ℓ coefficients, the universal coefficient (Bockstein) sequence and ℓ-adic completion (Weibel IV §2). The universal property of the plus construction, the concrete spectrum model and stable homotopy category, the Milnor lim¹ and exact-couple convergence proofs, and several imported topology lemmas (Dold–Lashof, Milnor, Segal, Tornehave) remain unread boundaries recorded as gaps.

nodes.title: Nerve, classifying space and its cell structure
nodes.statement: For a small category C, the nerve NC is the simplicial set whose p-simplices are strings X₀ → X₁ → ⋯ → X_p of composable morphisms, with i-th face deleting X_i and i-th degeneracy inserting an identity; BC = |NC| is a CW complex whose p-cells correspond to the nondegenerate p-simplices (no arrow an identity). A functor induces a cellular map, giving a faithful (not full) functor from small categories to CW complexes. There is a canonical cellular homeomorphism BC ≅ B(C^op) not induced by a functor, and B(C × C′) → BC × BC′ is a homeomorphism if one factor is a finite complex or if the product is given the compactly generated topology. For a partially ordered set the realization is the simplicial complex of its finite chains; for a group G viewed as a one-object category, BG is a K(G,1).
hypotheses: C is small (its objects form a set); for a skeletally small category such as finitely generated projective modules one realizes an equivalent small category, and any two choices give homotopy equivalent realizations (Weibel IV Example 3.2.1).
The product comparison needs either a finite factor or the compactly generated product topology.
proofSteps: Define NC with faces and degeneracies as above and take geometric realization; the recipe attaches one n-simplex for each string of n composable non-identity morphisms (Weibel IV Recipe 3.1.1, Definition 3.1.4).
The cellular homeomorphism with the opposite category comes from reversing each string; it is not realized by a functor except in special cases such as groups (Quillen §1 (3)).
Product compatibility is imported from Milnor's theorem on realizations of products (Quillen §1 (4), citing Milnor 1957); this imported proof was not read.
For a group G, Lemma 3.4 with the empty tree gives π₁(BG) = G; vanishing of higher homotopy groups is Weibel IV Exercise 3.2 (universal cover B(∫_G G) contractible), stated with a hint only.
acceptance: B(n) is the standard (n−1)-simplex and B of the two-element group is RP^∞ (Weibel IV Example 3.1.2).
The realization of a poset of simplices of a simplicial complex is its barycentric subdivision (Quillen §1, LNM p. 89).
Do not identify BC × BC′ with B(C × C′) in the ordinary product topology without the finiteness hypothesis.

nodes.title: Natural transformations give homotopies; adjoints and initial objects
nodes.statement: A natural transformation θ: f → g between functors C → C′ induces a homotopy BC × I → BC′ between Bf and Bg. Consequently a functor admitting a left or right adjoint is a homotopy equivalence, an equivalence of small categories is a homotopy equivalence, and a category with an initial or a final object is contractible (so every comma category C/d and d\C is contractible).
hypotheses: C, C′ small categories.
Uses the homeomorphism B(C × [1]) ≅ BC × B[1], valid because B[1] = I is a finite complex.
proofSteps: View (f, g, θ) as a functor C × [1] → C′, where [1] is the ordered set {0 < 1}; realize and use B[1] = I with the product homeomorphism (Quillen Prop. 2).
If f′ is left adjoint to f, the unit and counit give natural transformations f′f → id and id → ff′, so Bf′ is a homotopy inverse of Bf (Quillen Prop. 2 Cor. 1).
A category with an initial or final object has an adjoint to the functor to the one-point category (Quillen Prop. 2 Cor. 2).
acceptance: The comma category C/d has terminal object id_d and is contractible (Weibel IV Example 3.2.2).
An additive category, having zero as initial object, has contractible realization; the interesting space is B(iso A) (Weibel IV §4 opening).

nodes.title: Filtered colimits of small categories
nodes.statement: Let I be a filtering small category and i ↦ C_i a functor to small categories with colimit C, and choose compatible objects X_i with common image X. Then colim_i π_n(C_i, X_i) ≅ π_n(C, X). If every transition functor C_i → C_{i′} is a homotopy equivalence then each C_i → C is a homotopy equivalence. Every filtering category is contractible.
hypotheses: I is filtering (non-empty and directed).
The final Whitehead-theorem step needs CW complexes, which classifying spaces are.
proofSteps: Filtered colimits commute with finite limits, so NC = colim NC_i; a simplicial subset with finitely many nondegenerate simplices lifts to some NC_i, uniquely after enlarging i (Quillen Prop. 3 proof).
Every compact subset of a CW complex lies in a finite subcomplex, so compact subsets of BC lift, giving the colimit formula for homotopy groups.
For Corollary 1 replace I by the cofinal category i\I with initial object i; the map BC_i → BC is a weak equivalence, hence a homotopy equivalence by Whitehead's theorem.
I is the colimit of i ↦ I/i and each I/i has a final object, so I is contractible (Quillen Prop. 3 Cor. 2).
acceptance: A mapping telescope category ∫_{∪n} C has realization homotopy equivalent to B(colim C_n) (Weibel IV Exercise 3.5).
Do not apply the corollary when transition functors are not homotopy equivalences.

nodes.title: π₀, π₁, coverings and local coefficient systems of BC
nodes.statement: π₀(BC) is the set of objects modulo the equivalence relation generated by the existence of a morphism. The category of covering spaces of BC is equivalent to the category of morphism-inverting functors C → Sets, equivalently functors C[C⁻¹] → Sets from the groupoid obtained by formally inverting all arrows; hence π₁(BC, X) is canonically the automorphism group of X in C[C⁻¹], and a local coefficient system of abelian groups on BC is a morphism-inverting functor C → Ab. For connected C and a maximal tree T, π₁(BC) is generated by symbols [f] for morphisms f modulo [t] = 1 for t ∈ T, [id] = 1 and [f][g] = [f∘g].
hypotheses: C small; the maximal-tree presentation assumes C connected and non-empty (maximal trees exist by Zorn's lemma).
proofSteps: A covering E of BC gives a functor X ↦ E(X) sending arrows to bijections by path lifting along 1-cells (Quillen §1, LNM p. 90).

Conversely, for F morphism-inverting, the forgetful functor F\C → C (the Grothendieck construction ∫F) realizes to a map with fibre F(X); local triviality is imported from Gabriel–Zisman App. I 3.2 (not read).

The functor C → C[C⁻¹] induces an equivalence on morphism-inverting functor categories (Gabriel–Zisman I 1.2, not read); for connected C, C[C⁻¹] is equivalent to the automorphism group G_X, so coverings correspond to G_X-sets and π₁ = G_X by covering space theory.
The maximal-tree presentation is an application of van Kampen's theorem to the 2-skeleton (Weibel IV Lemma 3.4, proof indicated).
acceptance: For a group G regarded as a one-object category, π₁(BG) = G (Weibel IV Application 3.4.1); for a monoid M, π₁(BM) is the group completion of M (Application 3.4.2).
For H ⊂ G, the homotopy fibre of BH → BG is the discrete set G/H while the fibre category ι⁻¹(*) is a point (Weibel IV Exercise 3.3).

nodes.title: Homology of a small category and of its classifying space
nodes.statement: For a functor A: C → Ab let H_p(C, A) be the homology of the simplicial abelian group p ↦ ⊕_{X₀→⋯→X_p} A(X₀) (normalized chains). Then H_p(C, A) ≅ L_p colim^C(A), the left derived functors of colim: Funct(C, Ab) → Ab, with H₀(C, A) = colim A. For a local coefficient system L (a morphism-inverting functor), H_p(BC, L) ≅ H_p(C, L), and dually for cohomology with derived limits. For a discrete group G and G-module M this recovers group homology H_*(BG; M) = H_*(G; M), and H₁(BG; Z) = G/[G, G].
hypotheses: C small; the comparison with singular homology of BC is for coefficients forming a local system, i.e. morphism-inverting functors.
proofSteps: A ↦ H_*(C, A) is an exact δ-functor agreeing with colim in degree 0 and effaceable in positive degrees, hence equals the derived functors (Quillen §1, citing Gabriel–Zisman App. II 3.3, not read).

Filter BC by skeleta; the resulting spectral sequence has E¹_{pq} = 0 for q ≠ 0 and E¹_{*0} the normalized chain complex, so it degenerates to the local-coefficient comparison (Quillen §1, compare Segal 1968 §5.1, not read).
For G a one-object category the cellular chain complex of BG is the canonical bar complex computing group homology (Weibel IV 3.4.2 and 3.5, citing [WHomo 6.10.5, 8.2.3]).
acceptance: H₀(C; M) is the cokernel description of colim M (Weibel IV 3.5).
H₁(BG; Z) is the abelianization of G (roadmap H.1 test).
Group homology with nontrivial coefficients is required for acyclic maps; trivial-coefficient cohomology does not suffice (see H.3/acyclic-map-homology-criterion).

nodes.title: Homotopy fibre, homotopy-cartesian squares and the exact homotopy sequence
nodes.statement: For a map g: E → B and b ∈ B the homotopy fibre is F(g, b) = E ×_B B^I ×_B {b}, the space of pairs (e, γ) with γ a path from g(e) to b. For e ∈ g⁻¹(b) there is a long exact sequence ⋯ → π_{i+1}(B, b) → π_i(F(g, b), ē) → π_i(E, e) → π_i(B, b) → ⋯ ending in pointed sets π₁(B) → π₀(F) → π₀(E) → π₀(B). A commutative square E′ → E over B′ → B is homotopy-cartesian if E′ → B′ ×_B B^I ×_B E is a homotopy equivalence; if B′ is contractible this holds iff E′ → F(g, h(b′)) is a homotopy equivalence. A functor f: C → C′ and an object Y give a canonical map B(Y\f) → F(Bf, Y) from the natural transformation Y → fj.
hypotheses: The degree-0 and degree-1 terms are pointed sets and groups respectively; when E → B is an H-map of H-spaces F is an H-space and the terms are product preserving (Weibel IV 1.2).
Spaces of CW homotopy type are needed to turn weak equivalences into homotopy equivalences (Quillen §1 citing Milnor 1959).
proofSteps: Define F(g, b) and the comparison map from the strict fibre (Quillen §1, LNM p. 96).
The long exact sequence is the classical sequence of a fibration applied to the path-space replacement; its proof is imported from standard homotopy theory ([Wh]) and was not re-read.

For Y\f, the forgetful functor j: Y\f → C and the transformation (X, v) ↦ v: Y → fX give a canonical contraction of Bf∘Bj to Y, hence the canonical map to the homotopy fibre (Quillen §1, LNM p. 96; Weibel IV Example 3.2.3).

nodes.title: Realization of bisimplicial spaces
nodes.statement: For a bisimplicial space T, realizing first in q then in p, first in p then in q, and realizing the diagonal simplicial space p ↦ T_pp give spaces related by homeomorphisms functorial in T. In particular the realization of a bisimplicial set is homeomorphic to the realization of its diagonal.
hypotheses: Realization of simplicial spaces is defined as the left adjoint of Y ↦ (p ↦ Hom(Δ^p, Y)), so it commutes with colimits.
The representable case uses the product homeomorphism |Δ^r × Δ^s| ≅ Δ^r × Δ^s from the theory of realizations of products.
proofSteps: Check the three realizations agree functorially on bisimplicial spaces of the form h^{rs} × S = Hom(−, r) × Hom(−, s) × S, using |Hom(·, r) × Hom(·, s) × S| = Δ^r × Δ^s × S.
Every T has a canonical presentation as the coequalizer of ⊔ h^{r′s′} × T_rs ⇉ ⊔ h^{rs} × T_rs → T.
All three functors commute with colimits, so the homeomorphisms extend from representables to all T (Quillen §1 Lemma).
acceptance: The diagonal of the bisimplicial set T(f) in the proof of Theorem A is the nerve of S(f).
The realization of the product bicategory A ⊗ B is BA × BB (Weibel IV Example 3.10.1).

nodes.title: Quillen's quasi-fibration lemma for diagrams of spaces over a nerve
nodes.statement: Let I be a small category and i ↦ X_i a functor to topological spaces, and let g: X_I → BI be the realization of the map from p ↦ ⊔_{i₀→⋯→i_p} X_{i₀} to the nerve of I. If every induced map X_i → X_{i′} is a homotopy equivalence then g is a quasi-fibration: for every b ∈ BI the map g⁻¹(b) → F(g, b) induces isomorphisms on homotopy groups. When the spaces involved have CW homotopy type the square g⁻¹(b) → X_I over {b} → BI is homotopy-cartesian.
hypotheses: Every transition map X_i → X_{i′} (for arrows i → i′ of I) is a homotopy equivalence.
Homotopy-cartesian conclusion requires CW homotopy types (Milnor 1959, cited, not read).
proofSteps: By Dold–Lashof Lemma 1.5 it suffices to show g restricted to each skeleton F_p of BI is a quasi-fibration (imported, not read).

Let U be F_p minus the barycentres of the p-cells and V = F_p − F_{p−1}; by Dold–Lashof Lemma 1.4 it suffices to treat U, V and U ∩ V (imported, not read); over each open p-cell g is a product, which handles V and U ∩ V.
For U apply Dold–Lashof Lemma 1.3 (imported, not read) using induction on p and the radial fibre-preserving deformation of Δ^p minus its barycentre onto ∂Δ^p.

If the deformation moves x in the cell of i₀ → ⋯ → i_p to the face with vertices j₀ < ⋯ < j_q, then g⁻¹(x) = X_{i₀}, g⁻¹(x′) = X_{k₀} with k₀ = i_{j₀}, and the induced map is the transition map of i₀ → k₀, a homotopy equivalence by hypothesis (Quillen §1 Lemma proof).
acceptance: Applied to Y ↦ B(Y\f) under the hypothesis of Theorem B, yields that BS(f) → BC′^op is a quasi-fibration.
Applied to contractible fibres (Y\f contractible or C′/fX with a final object), yields the levelwise equivalences in the proof of Theorem A.
The Dold–Lashof lemmas must be supplied or sourced before this node is proof-complete.

nodes.title: Quillen's Theorem A
nodes.statement: Let f: C → C′ be a functor between small categories. If the comma category Y\f of pairs (X, v: Y → fX) is contractible for every object Y of C′, then f is a homotopy equivalence. Dually, it suffices that every f/Y be contractible. If f is prefibred or precofibred and every fibre f⁻¹(Y) is contractible, f is a homotopy equivalence.
hypotheses: C, C′ small.
For the corollary: f prefibred (each f⁻¹(Y) → Y\f has a right adjoint) or precofibred (each f⁻¹(Y) → f/Y has a left adjoint).
proofSteps: Form S(f), the category of triples (X, Y, v: Y → fX), with functors p₁: S(f) → C and p₂: S(f) → C′^op; it is the cofibred category over C × C′^op defined by (X, Y) ↦ Hom(Y, fX).
Let T(f) be the bisimplicial set of pairs (Y_p → ⋯ → Y₀ → fX₀, X₀ → ⋯ → X_q); its diagonal is NS(f) (bisimplicial realization lemma), and forgetting the first component realizes to Bp₁.

Realizing in p gives, in each q, ⊔_{X₀→⋯→X_q} B(C′/fX₀)^op → NC_q, a homotopy equivalence since C′/fX₀ has a final object; by the quasi-fibration lemma (or Tornehave A.3) Bp₁ is a homotopy equivalence.
Realizing T(f) → N(C′^op) in q gives fibres B(Y₀\f), contractible by hypothesis, so p₂ is a homotopy equivalence.

Compare with f = id_{C′} through S(f) → S(id_{C′}), (X, Y, v) ↦ (fX, Y, v), compatible with p₁ and p₂; since Y\id_{C′} has an initial object the same argument applies, and two-out-of-three gives Bf a homotopy equivalence.
For the corollary, the adjoint gives B(f⁻¹(Y)) ≃ B(Y\f) (Quillen §1, Prop. 2 Cor. 1).
acceptance: A simplicial map of simplicial complexes whose inverse image of every closed simplex is contractible is a homotopy equivalence (Quillen's example).
The inclusion of monoids N → Z gives BN ≃ BZ ≃ S¹ (Weibel IV Example 3.7.2).
Source and target functors from the arrow category (Segal subdivision) are homotopy equivalences (Quillen's example after the corollary; Weibel IV Exercises 3.9, 3.12).

nodes.title: Quillen's Theorem B
nodes.statement: Let f: C → C′ be a functor such that for every arrow u: Y → Y′ of C′ the induced functor u*: Y′\f → Y\f is a homotopy equivalence. Then for every object Y of C′ the square with Y\f → C over Y\C′ → C′ is homotopy-cartesian, so B(Y\f) is homotopy equivalent to the homotopy fibre of Bf over Y, and for X ∈ f⁻¹(Y) there is an exact sequence ⋯ → π_{i+1}(C′, Y) → π_i(Y\f, (X, id_Y)) → π_i(C, X) → π_i(C′, Y) → ⋯. Dually with f/Y. If f is prefibred and every base change u*: f⁻¹(Y′) → f⁻¹(Y) is a homotopy equivalence (or precofibred with cobase changes homotopy equivalences), the fibre f⁻¹(Y) is homotopy equivalent to the homotopy fibre of f over Y.
hypotheses: Every transition functor Y′\f → Y\f (respectively every base change or cobase change) is a homotopy equivalence; contractibility of comma categories alone (Theorem A) does not produce a fibration sequence.
Spaces have CW homotopy type so that quasi-fibrations give homotopy-cartesian squares.

nodes.title: Acyclic spaces, acyclic maps and plus constructions
nodes.statement: A space F is acyclic if its reduced integral homology vanishes; then F is connected, G = π₁(F) is perfect and H₂(G; Z) = 0. A map f: X → Y of based connected CW complexes is acyclic if its homotopy fibre F(f) is acyclic; then π₁(X) → π₁(Y) is surjective with perfect normal kernel P. An acyclic map f: X → Y is a plus construction on X relative to a perfect normal subgroup P ⊂ π₁(X) if P is the kernel of π₁(X) → π₁(Y).
hypotheses: X, Y based connected CW complexes.
Lemma 1.3.1 uses the Serre spectral sequence of the universal-cover fibration F̃ → F → BG and its low-degree exact sequence.
proofSteps: H₀(F) = Z gives connectedness; G/[G, G] = H₁(F; Z) = 0 gives perfectness (Weibel IV Lemma 1.3.1).

The homotopy fibre of F → BG is the universal cover F̃, with H₁(F̃; Z) = 0; the Serre spectral sequence E²_{pq} = H_p(G; H_q(F̃; Z)) ⇒ H_{p+q}(F; Z) gives H₂(F) → H₂(G) → H₁(F̃)_G, hence H₂(G; Z) = 0.
For an acyclic map, exactness of π₁F(f) → π₁X → π₁Y → π₀F(f) with F(f) connected gives surjectivity, and the kernel is the image of the perfect group π₁F(f) (Weibel IV Definition 1.4).
acceptance: The Volodin space X(R) ⊂ BGL(R) is acyclic with π₁ image E(R) (Weibel IV Example 1.3.2, cited from Suslin).
Applying the plus construction to an acyclic space gives a contractible space (Weibel IV Exercise 1.2(a)).
Group homology with nontrivial local coefficients, not trivial-coefficient cohomology, defines acyclicity (roadmap H.1).

nodes.title: Acyclic maps are local-coefficient homology isomorphisms
nodes.statement: A map f: X → Y of connected CW complexes is acyclic if and only if H_*(X; M) → H_*(Y; M) is an isomorphism for every π₁(Y)-module M (pulled back to X).
hypotheses: X, Y connected CW complexes; M ranges over all π₁(Y)-modules, including Z[π₁Y].
Uses the Serre spectral sequence with local coefficients and its comparison theorem.
proofSteps: If f is acyclic, π₁F(f) → π₁Y is trivial, so π₁F(f) acts trivially on M and H_q(F(f); M) = 0 for q ≠ 0 by universal coefficients; the Serre spectral sequence H_p(Y; H_q(F(f); M)) ⇒ H_{p+q}(X; M) collapses.
Conversely, if π₁Y = 0 and f is an integral homology isomorphism, comparing the Serre spectral sequences of F(f) → X → Y and ∗ → Y → Y gives H̃_*(F(f); Z) = 0.

In general pass to the universal cover Ỹ and X̃ = X ×_Y Ỹ: H_*(Ỹ; Z) ≅ H_*(Y; Z[π₁Y]) and H_*(X̃; Z) ≅ H_*(X; Z[π₁Y]), so X̃ → Ỹ is an integral homology isomorphism with simply connected target, and F(f̃) ≅ F(f) by path lifting (Weibel IV Lemma 1.6 proof).
acceptance: An integral homology isomorphism with non-perfect kernel on π₁ is not acyclic; test with a map inducing an isomorphism on integral homology only.
The comparison must be proved for Z[π₁Y] coefficients, not only for trivial modules.

nodes.title: Existence of the plus construction by attaching 2- and 3-cells
nodes.statement: If X is a connected CW complex with H₁(X) = 0, there are a simply connected CW complex X⁺ and an inclusion X → X⁺ inducing isomorphisms on all integral homology groups. More generally, for a connected CW complex X and a perfect subgroup H ⊂ π₁(X), there is a CW complex X⁺ and a map X → X⁺ such that π₁(X) → π₁(X⁺) is surjective with kernel the normal subgroup generated by H and X → X⁺ is an isomorphism on integral homology.
hypotheses: X connected CW complex; H ⊂ π₁(X) perfect (normality is not assumed; the kernel is the normal closure).

The source proves integral homology isomorphism only; the local-coefficient isomorphism (equivalently acyclicity, by Lemma 1.6) required by Weibel IV Definition 1.1(2) is not proved in the passages read.
proofSteps: For H₁(X) = 0: attach 2-cells along loops generating π₁(X) to get a simply connected X′; since H₁(X) = 0 the sequence 0 → H₂(X) → H₂(X′) → H₂(X′, X) → 0 splits, with H₂(X′, X) free on the 2-cells (Hatcher Prop. 4.40).
By Hurewicz H₂(X′) ≅ π₂(X′); represent a basis of the free summand by cellular maps S² → X′ and attach 3-cells along them, giving simply connected X⁺ with X → X⁺ a homology isomorphism.
For perfect H ⊂ π₁(X): take the covering p: X̃ → X with π₁(X̃) ≅ H, so H₁(X̃) = 0, apply the first case to X̃, and glue X̃⁺ to the mapping cylinder M_p along X̃.
Van Kampen gives π₁(X) → π₁(X⁺) surjective with kernel the normal closure of H; X⁺/M_p ≅ X̃⁺/X̃ gives H_*(X⁺, M_p) = H_*(X̃⁺, X̃) = 0, so X → X⁺ is an integral homology isomorphism.
Weibel IV Exercise 1.4 gives an alternative outline for normal perfect P attaching one 2-cell per element of P and matching 3-cells; its homology claims are stated as an exercise.
acceptance: Plus construction relative to the trivial subgroup is a homotopy equivalence (roadmap H.3 test); for a perfect group the result is simply connected with the same integral homology.
For the Poincaré homology sphere X = S³/SL₂(F₅), S³ → X⁺ is a homotopy equivalence (Weibel IV Exercise 1.1).

nodes.title: Universal property and uniqueness of the plus construction (unread proof boundary)
nodes.statement: Recorded statement (Weibel IV Theorem 1.5, Quillen): for a perfect normal subgroup P of π₁(X), (1) a plus construction f: X → Y relative to P exists; (2) for any map g: X → Z with P mapping trivially to π₁(Z) there is h: Y → Z, unique up to homotopy, with g = hf; (3) any two plus constructions relative to P are homotopy equivalent under X. nodes.title: π₂ of a plus construction and universal central extensions
nodes.statement: Let P be a perfect normal subgroup of a group G and f: BG → BG⁺ the plus construction relative to P, with homotopy fibre F(f). Then π₁F(f) is the universal central extension of P and π₂(BG⁺) ≅ H₂(P; Z). For G = GL(R), P = E(R) this identifies π₂BGL(R)⁺ with H₂(E(R); Z), the kernel of the Steinberg extension. Moreover BP⁺ is homotopy equivalent to the universal cover of BG⁺, so π_n(BP⁺) ≅ π_n(BG⁺) for n ≥ 2, and for a universal central extension A → S → P there is a homotopy fibration BA → BS⁺ → BP⁺ with π_n(BS⁺) = 0 for n ≤ 2 and π₃(BP⁺) ≅ H₃(S; Z).
hypotheses: P perfect normal in G; for the Steinberg application E(R) is perfect and St(R) → E(R) is its universal central extension (Weibel III.5.5, not read here).
The last two assertions are Weibel IV Exercises 1.8 and 1.9, stated with hints and not proved in the source.
proofSteps: The homotopy sequence gives π₂(BG) = 0 → π₂(BG⁺) → π₁F(f) → G → G/P → 1, so π₁F(f) is an extension of P by π₂(BG⁺).
π₂(BG⁺) is central in π₁F(f) ([Wh IV.3.5], imported).
F(f) is acyclic, so π₁F(f) is perfect with H₂ = 0 (H.3/acyclic-spaces-and-maps).

The recognition theorem for universal central extensions (Weibel III.5.4, not read here) identifies π₁F(f) as the universal central extension of P, whose kernel is H₂(P; Z) (Weibel IV Proposition 1.7).
Exercises 1.8–1.9: BP is homotopy equivalent to a covering of BG; apply the plus construction and Hurewicz in the first nonzero degree (hints only).

nodes.title: Quillen's S⁻¹S construction for a symmetric monoidal groupoid
nodes.statement: For a symmetric monoidal category (S, □, e), BS is a homotopy-commutative, homotopy-associative H-space and B(iso S) ≃ ⊔ B Aut(s) over isomorphism classes. Assume every morphism of S is an isomorphism and translations Aut(s) → Aut(s□t) are injective. S⁻¹S has objects pairs (m, n) and morphisms equivalence classes of composites (m₁, m₂) → (s□m₁, s□m₂) → (n₁, n₂), two composites being equivalent when an isomorphism α: s ≅ t identifies their second parts. S⁻¹S is symmetric monoidal, m ↦ (m, e) is monoidal, π₀(S⁻¹S) is an abelian group, and K₀(S) = π₀(S⁻¹S) is the group completion of the monoid π₀(S) = S^iso; K_n(S) = π_n B(S⁻¹S).
hypotheses: S symmetric monoidal with coherence isomorphisms satisfying the pentagon, hexagon and unit conditions (Carlsson Definition 7); direct sum is not assumed strictly associative.
Every morphism an isomorphism and translations faithful, needed for Theorem 4.8 and for morphisms of S⁻¹S to determine s, f, g up to unique isomorphism.
proofSteps: Define the H-space structure on BS from B(□): BS × BS ≅ B(S × S) → BS (compactly generated product) and the coherence isomorphisms (Weibel IV §4 opening).
Define S⁻¹S and its composition; with faithful translations each morphism determines s, f and g up to unique isomorphism (Explanation 4.2.1).
The inverse of (m, n) in π₀ is (n, m), using a morphism (e, e) → (m□n, n□m); this is not natural (Remark 4.2.2 and Exercise 4.3).
Lemma 4.3.1: α(m, n) = [m] − [n] is constant on components, giving an inverse to the universal map from the group completion of π₀(S).
acceptance: Pic(R) with π₀ already a group gives K₀ = Pic(R), K₁ = R^× and K_n = 0 for n ≥ 2 (Weibel IV Example 4.4.2).
There is no natural transformation 0 ⇒ id□ι on S⁻¹S (Weibel IV Exercise 4.3): the homotopy inverse is not given by a natural transformation.
Do not use the nerve of all projective-module maps; BP(R) is contractible, only iso P(R) carries the group completion input.

nodes.title: Quillen's theorem: S⁻¹X localizes homology; B(S⁻¹S) is a group completion
nodes.statement: Let S be a symmetric monoidal category in which every map is an isomorphism and translations are faithful, acting on a category X (s□(t□x) ≅ (s□t)□x, e□x ≅ x coherently), and let S⁻¹X = ⟨S, S × X⟩. Then the map (π₀S)⁻¹H_q(X) → H_q(S⁻¹X) induced by x ↦ (e, x) is an isomorphism for all q. In particular B(S⁻¹S) is a group completion of BS: an H-space map inducing the group completion on π₀ and H_*(B(S⁻¹S); k) ≅ π₀(S)⁻¹H_*(BS; k) for every commutative ring k.
hypotheses: Every map in S is an isomorphism; translations Aut(s) → Aut(s□t) are injective.
Group completion in Definition 4.4 is defined for homotopy commutative, homotopy associative H-spaces; for CW complexes the completion is group-like.
proofSteps: The projection ρ: S⁻¹X → ⟨S, S⟩, (s, x) ↦ s, is cofibred with fibre X (Weibel IV Exercise 4.5, statement only).
A cofibred functor yields a spectral sequence E²_{pq} = H_p(⟨S, S⟩; H_q(X)) ⇒ H_{p+q}(S⁻¹X) from the double complex of pairs of strings (Weibel IV Exercise 3.7, statement with construction hint).
Localizing at the multiplicative set π₀S ⊂ H₀(S) is exact and π₀S already acts invertibly on H_*(S⁻¹X), giving E²_{pq} = H_p(⟨S, S⟩; M_q) with M_q = (π₀S)⁻¹H_q(X).

Each M_q is morphism-inverting, hence a local system (H.1 coverings node), and ⟨S, S⟩ is contractible because e is initial; so H_p(⟨S, S⟩; M_q) vanishes for p ≠ 0 and the spectral sequence degenerates (Weibel IV Theorem 4.8 proof, following Grayson's 'Higher algebraic K-theory II', p. 221, not read).
The group completion statement follows with Remark 4.2.2 and Lemma 4.3.1.
acceptance: K₁(S) = colim_s H₁(Aut(s); Z) (Weibel IV Corollary 4.8.1).
Barratt–Priddy–Quillen–Segal: for finite sets K(Sets_fin) ≃ Z × BΣ_∞⁺ (Weibel IV 4.9.2–4.9.3; the identification with Ω^∞S^∞ is cited, not proved).

nodes.title: Group completions of H-spaces: group-like case and uniqueness up to phantom maps
nodes.statement: If X is a group-like H-space, X is its own group completion and every group completion X → Y is a homotopy equivalence. In general group completions are not unique up to homotopy when phantom maps exist; if π₀(X) is countable or has a countable cofinal submonoid, any two group completions X → X′, X → X″ are related by a homotopy equivalence g: X′ → X″, unique up to weak homotopy, with gf′ weakly homotopic to f″.
hypotheses: H-spaces of CW type; countability of π₀(X) or of a cofinal submonoid for the uniqueness theorem.
proofSteps: A group completion of a group-like X is a homology isomorphism, hence an isomorphism on π₀ and π₁; on basepoint components it is a plus construction relative to the trivial subgroup, so Theorem 1.5 gives a homotopy equivalence (Weibel IV Lemma 4.4.1; depends on H.3/plus-construction-universal-property).
If f: X → Y is a group completion and φ is phantom, f + φ is again a group completion (Weibel IV p. 39).
The uniqueness theorem is quoted from Caradus–Clarke–McGibbon–Thomason [CCMT, 1.2]; its proof was not read (source boundary).

nodes.title: B(S⁻¹S) ≃ Z × BGL(R)⁺ for based free modules
nodes.statement: For a ring R let S = F(R) = ⊔_n GL_n(R), the symmetric monoidal groupoid of based free modules R^n under concatenation and block sum. Then B(S⁻¹S) is the group completion of BS and B(S⁻¹S) ≃ Z × BGL(R)⁺. More generally, if S = iso S has faithful translations and a cofinal sequence s_{n+1} = s_n□a_n, then the commutator subgroup E of Aut(S) = colim Aut(s_n) is perfect normal, K₁(S) = Aut(S)/E, and K(S) ≃ K₀(S) × B Aut(S)⁺.

The product decomposition is a space-level statement after choosing component representatives; it is not a natural splitting of infinite loop spaces (Weibel IV 1.1.2).

By Theorem 4.8, H_*(B(S⁻¹S)) is the localization of H_*(BS) at {e^n}, i.e. the colimit along ⊕R, so H_*(B(S⁻¹S)) ≅ H_*(Y_S) ⊗ Z[e, e⁻¹] with H_*(Y_S) ≅ colim H_*(BGL_n(R)) = H_*(BGL(R)).
Thus BGL(R) → Y_S is an integral homology isomorphism into an H-space, so Remark 1.8.1 (H.3 universal-property boundary) gives BGL(R)⁺ ≃ Y_S.
For Theorem 4.10 the telescope gives an acyclic map from B Aut(S) to the basepoint component, which is by definition a plus construction.

nodes.title: Segal's Γ-space construction from categories with sums
nodes.statement: A Γ-space is a functor F from Γ^op (finite based sets) to simplicial sets with F(∅₊) weakly contractible and F(n) → ∏_{i=1}^n F(1) (induced by the projections p_i) a weak equivalence. For a category C with a zero object and categorical sums, Sum_C(X) is the category of summing functors Π(X) → C (φ(∅) a zero object and φ(S) ⊕ φ(T) → φ(S ∪ T) an isomorphism when S ∩ T = {∗}) with natural isomorphisms; Sp₁(C) = N∘Sum_C(−) is a Γ-space, iterating gives Sp_n(C) and maps σ_n: Sp_n(C) → ΩSp_{n+1}(C). Segal's theorem (quoted): σ_n are weak equivalences for n > 1 as printed, σ₀ is a group completion, and the construction gives a functor to spectra; for finite sets it gives the sphere spectrum, for finitely generated projective modules the K-theory spectrum.
hypotheses: C has a zero object and categorical sums, and functors preserve them; symmetric monoidal categories without categorical sums (such as iso P(R)) require the May–Thomason extension, not read.
The printed statement of Theorem 3 says 'for n > 1'; the case n = 1 must be checked against Segal's original before use.
proofSteps: Sum_C(f)(φ)(S) = φ(f⁻¹(S)) makes Sum_C a functor Γ^op → CAT (Carlsson §1.2).

Proposition 2: Sum_C(∅) is the contractible category of zero objects; the functor Sum_C(n) → ∏ Sum_C(1) is an equivalence with inverse θ(φ₁, …, φ_n)({i₁, …, i_s}) = φ_{i₁}(1) ⊕ ⋯ ⊕ φ_{i_s}(1) (proof given).
Sum_C(X) again has zero objects and sums, so the construction iterates; SumC(1) ≃ C gives ΣN.C → Sp₁(C) and adjoints σ_n.
Theorem 3 (Segal 1974, 'Categories and cohomology theories') is quoted without proof in Carlsson; its proof is an unread boundary.

nodes.title: Ω-spectra, homotopy groups and Eilenberg–Mac Lane spectra from the bar construction
nodes.statement: A spectrum (in the sequential model used by the K-theory sources) is a family of based spaces {X_i}_{i≥0} with bonding maps σ_i: X_i → ΩX_{i+1}; an Ω-spectrum has σ_i homotopy equivalences, and it is connective if π_n = 0 for n < 0. Its homotopy groups are π_n(E) = colim_r π_{n+r}(E_r), defined for all n ∈ Z. For an abelian group A the bar construction B.A (B_kA = A^k with the displayed faces) is a simplicial abelian group; iterating gives n-simplicial abelian groups B^n.A with exact sequences B^{n−1}.A → E^n.A → B^n.A, E^n.A contractible, which realize to fibrations, so |B^{n−1}.A| ≃ Ω|B^n.A| and {B^n.A} is the Eilenberg–Mac Lane spectrum of A.
hypotheses: A abelian (so that B.A is a simplicial abelian group and the construction iterates).
The fibration property of exact sequences of simplicial abelian groups is imported, not proved in the passage read.
proofSteps: Define faces d₀, d_i (adding adjacent entries) and d_k on A^k; commutativity makes multiplication a homomorphism, so B.A is a simplicial abelian group (Carlsson §1.2).
Apply B. degreewise to obtain B^n.A and restrict to the diagonal.
Quote: exact sequences of simplicial abelian groups realize to Serre fibrations, and E^n.A is contractible, giving |B^{n−1}.A| ≃ Ω|B^n.A| (Carlsson §1.2; proof imported, not read).
The stable homotopy category, stable equivalences, fibrant replacement and the fibre/cofibre shift are not constructed in the sources read (see gaps).
acceptance: π_n of the Eilenberg–Mac Lane spectrum of A is A in degree 0 and zero otherwise.
Weibel IV 8.5.5: the S.-construction gives a connective Ω-spectrum with π_i = K_i for i ≥ 0.
Negative homotopy groups of a spectrum depend on the chosen deloopings (Weibel IV §2 remark on K_m(R; Z/ℓ) for m < 2).

nodes.title: The iterated S.-construction is a connective Ω-spectrum
nodes.statement: For a small Waldhausen category C with K(C) = Ω|wS.C| and π₁|wS.C| ≅ K₀(C), the sequence of spaces Ω|wS.C|, |wS.C|, |wS.S.C|, …, |wS.^nC|, … with the maps |wS.^nC| → Ω|wS.^{n+1}C| forms a connective Ω-spectrum KC with π_i(KC) = K_i(C) for i ≥ 0. An exact functor induces a map of spectra, and a biexact functor A × B → C induces a pairing K(A) ∧ K(B) → K(C).
hypotheses: C small Waldhausen category; the S.-construction S_nC (with chosen subquotients, cofibrations and weak equivalences) is supplied by GeneralAlgebraicKTheory:K.4:construction.
The homotopy-fibration step uses the fibration sequence of Weibel V.1.7, which rests on the Additivity Theorem; that proof is not read in this packet.
proofSteps: π₁ of a simplicial space X. with X₀ a point is the free group on π₀(X₁) modulo ∂₁x = ∂₂x·∂₀x; for X. = BwS.C this is K₀(C) (Weibel IV Proposition 8.4).
For an exact functor f: B → C define S_nf = S_nB ×_{S_nC} S_{n+1}C, a simplicial Waldhausen category containing C, with C → S.f → S.B (Weibel IV 8.5.3).
Lemma 8.5.4: for f = id_C, S.f is the simplicial path space of S.C and wS.S.f the path space of wS.S.C, contractible since S₀f = 0 (proof given).
The realization of wS.B → wS.C → wS.(S.f) → wS.(S.B) is a homotopy fibration sequence by Weibel V.1.7 (source boundary here; to be read with the Additivity Theorem).
Taking f = id gives |wS.C| ≃ Ω|wS.S.C|; iterating in the multisimplicial categories S.^nC gives the Ω-spectrum (Weibel IV 8.5.5).
Products: a biexact functor induces wS.A × wS.B → wwS.S.C, factoring through the smash product after realization (Weibel IV 8.11, sketched).
acceptance: For an exact category A with isomorphisms as weak equivalences, |iS.A| ≃ BQA (Waldhausen 1.9; Weibel IV Exercises 8.5–8.6, statements with hints).
Relative groups end with K₀(B) → K₀(C) → K₋₁(f) → 0 (Weibel IV Exercise 8.11).
A sequence of spaces without the fibration theorem does not count as the spectrum.

nodes.title: Mod-ℓ homotopy groups and the universal coefficient (Bockstein) sequence
nodes.statement: For m ≥ 2 let P^m(Z/ℓ) be the Moore space (S^{m−1} with an m-cell attached by a degree ℓ map) and π_m(X; Z/ℓ) = [P^m(Z/ℓ), X]. The cofibration S^{m−1} → S^{m−1} → P^m(Z/ℓ) gives an exact sequence π_m(X) → π_m(X) → π_m(X; Z/ℓ) → π_{m−1}(X) → π_{m−1}(X) (multiplication by ℓ), hence for m ≥ 3 a natural short exact sequence 0 → π_m(X) ⊗ Z/ℓ → π_m(X; Z/ℓ) → ℓπ_{m−1}(X) → 0, split but not naturally when ℓ ≢ 2 mod 4. For a spectrum or infinite loop space E the sequence holds for all m ∈ Z, with π_*(E; Z/ℓ) the homotopy of E ∧ P^∞(Z/ℓ), and for K-theory 0 → K_m(C) ⊗ Z/ℓ → K_m(C; Z/ℓ) → ℓK_{m−1}(C) → 0 is split unless ℓ ≡ 2 mod 4, not naturally. If X is a loop space, π_m(X; Z/ℓ) ≅ π_{m−1}(F) for F the homotopy fibre of ℓ: X → X, and for coprime q₁q₂ = ℓ, π_m(X; Z/ℓ) ≅ π_m(X; Z/q₁) × π_m(X; Z/q₂).
hypotheses: m ≥ 2 for spaces (groups for m ≥ 3, abelian for m ≥ 4, improved by one for H-spaces); all m ∈ Z for spectra/infinite loop spaces with specified deloopings.
The splitting is non-canonical and fails for ℓ ≡ 2 mod 4.
proofSteps: Apply [−, X] to the defining cofibration sequence and use exactness of [P, F] → [P, E] → [P, B] for fibrations ([Wh III.6.18*], imported) (Weibel IV 2.1.1).
Rewrite the five-term sequence using the ℓ-torsion subgroup ℓA to obtain the universal coefficient sequence (Weibel IV 2.2).
Neisendorfer's proof of Proposition 2.3: Maps(−, X) turns the cofibration S^k → S^k → P^{k+1} into a fibration and Maps(S^k, −) preserves the fibration F → X → X; compare the two homotopy fibres.
Proposition 2.7: P = P^m(Z/q₁) ∨ P^m(Z/q₂) → P^m(Z/ℓ) is a homotopy equivalence because P has the single reduced homology group Z/q₁ × Z/q₂ ≅ Z/ℓ.
Spectrum version: the Moore spectrum is the cofibre of ℓ on the sphere spectrum and π_*(E; Z/ℓ) = colim π_{*+r}(E_r; Z/ℓ) = π_*(E ∧ P^∞(Z/ℓ)) by S-duality (Weibel IV 2.3.1, stated).
acceptance: Nonsplit example: π_{m+2}(S^m; Z/2) = Z/4 for m ≥ 3 and π₂(BO; Z/2) = Z/4 (Weibel IV Example 2.2.1).
K₂(Z; Z/2) ≅ Z/4 has a nonzero torsion right-hand term (Weibel IV Example 2.5.1).
The Bott element in K₂(R; Z/ℓ) depends on the chosen splitting (Weibel IV Remark 2.5.3).
Products on mod ℓ^ν groups are asserted only outside ℓ^ν = 2, 3, 4, 8 (Theorem 2.8; Araki–Toda input not read).

nodes.title: ℓ-adic completion of a spectrum and the lim¹ sequence
nodes.statement: For a prime ℓ and a spectrum E, the ℓ-adic completion is the homotopy limit over ν of E ∧ P^∞(Z/ℓ^ν), with homotopy groups π_n(E; Z_ℓ), and there is an extension 0 → lim¹_ν π_{n+1}(E; Z/ℓ^ν) → π_n(E; Z_ℓ) → lim_ν π_n(E; Z/ℓ^ν) → 0. If the groups π_{n+1}(E; Z/ℓ^ν) are finite the lim¹ term vanishes and π_n(E; Z_ℓ) is an extension of the ℓ-adic Tate module of π_{n−1}(E) by the ℓ-adic completion of π_n(E). Consequently π_n(E; Z_ℓ) agrees with π_n(E) ⊗ Z_ℓ only under additional hypotheses (for example π_n(E) finitely generated and vanishing Tate module of π_{n−1}(E)).
hypotheses: Homotopy limit of the tower E ∧ P^∞(Z/ℓ^ν) with the transition maps induced by the Moore spectra; finiteness of π_{n+1}(E; Z/ℓ^ν) for the vanishing of lim¹.
If E is a homotopy associative and commutative ring spectrum, so is its completion.
proofSteps: Define the completion as a homotopy limit of the tower (Weibel IV 2.9).
The lim¹ extension for the homotopy groups of a homotopy limit of a tower is quoted without proof (source boundary: Milnor sequence).
Finite groups satisfy the Mittag-Leffler condition, so lim¹ vanishes; combining lim_ν of the universal coefficient sequences 2.5 gives the Tate-module extension (Weibel IV 2.9 as stated).
acceptance: K₁(C; Z_ℓ) = Z_ℓ from the Tate module of C^× (Weibel IV 2.9).
Exhibit a tower with nonzero lim¹ before replacing completion by an inverse limit (roadmap H.6 acceptance).
Keep the Tate module term: completion is not tensoring with Z_ℓ in general.

In the atlas, GeneralAlgebraicKTheory:K.4 (which owns additivity) requires StableHomotopyKTheory:H.5:S-delooping. If the delooping proof needs additivity, the additivity theorem must be a separate node that precedes H.5:S-delooping. Not yet verified against Waldhausen §1.4–1.5; next action is in the GeneralAlgebraicKTheory packet.
